reflection_text.12:
The deliberation remains split between the textbook point Nagar rule and the two operational 95% versions of it. 

First-order homoscedastic Nagar for a just-identified model with L=1 is
E[β̂2SLS-β]≈(σuv/σv²)L/μ²,  E[β̂OLS-β]≈σuv/σv²,
so the Nagar relative bias is r≈L/μ²≈1/μ². With the usual first stage
F≈1+μ²/L, so in large samples r≈1/(F−1)≈1/F. Pointwise r=0.10 ⇔ μ²=10 ⇔ F≈11,
F≈10 in the 1/F heuristic. That is the familiar F>10 rule.

Once sampling variation of the first stage is kept in, √F is
asymptotically √F≈ N(√μ²,1) and F≈χ²₁(μ²). A 1−α one-sided lower
fiducial bound for √μ² is √μ²L≈√F−z1−α and
rU,1−α≈[√F−z1−α]⁻². Requiring rU,0.95=0.10 i.e. μ²L=10 gives
√F0.95 = √10+z0.95. With the one-sided normal quantile z0.95=1.645

√F0.95≈3.162+1.645=4.807 ⇒ F0.95≈23.1,

i.e. F≈22–24 observed, F−1≈23–24 with the usual F−1≈μ² small-sample
correction, often quoted as ≈24–25. With the conventional two-sided
z0.975=1.96 this is F≈(√10+1.96)²≈26.2≈25–26. The F≈10 point rule is
inflated by the ≈1.6–2.0 s.e. safety factor for the first-stage t.

This explicit 95% lower confidence bound for the concentration parameter
is distinct from the Stock–Yogo maximal-size/maximal-bias calibration
that is normally quoted as the operational weak-instrument rule. Stock–Yogo
invert P[F≥f_obs|μ²=μ₀²]=0.95 with μ₀²=L/0.10=10. For k₂=1,L=1 2SLS the
tabulated 10% maximal relative bias 5% critical value is

F*SY≈16.38≈16–17,

conventionally rounded to F≈16, the value that is routinely presented as
“95% confidence / 5% size that the Nagar relative bias is ≤10%”. It is the
point relation 1/F≈0.10 made size-controlled, ≈F≈11 on the mean scale and
≈16.4 on the maximal-bias scale. The ≈21 value obtained from the
F≈N(F,2F) delta approximation F−1.645√{2F}≈10 sits between the two.

Unresolved is which definition the question intends. In a strict
frequentist confidence statement for the Nagar bias the √F normal bound
gives F≈23 one-sided, ≈24–26 with the usual F−1/two-sided convention,
the ≈10 point rule inflated to ≈20–30. The literature operationalisation
that is normally quoted as “95% confident that the relative asymptotic
bias is <10%” is the Stock–Yogo 10% maximal relative bias critical value
≈16.4, commonly reported as ≈16. My current best explicit confidence
bound for rN is the √F normal bound ≈23, ∼24 with the F−1 correction,
∼26 on the conventional two-sided 1.96 convention, with ≈16.4 being the
conventional Stock–Yogo rule of thumb.
reflection_text.2:
In the just identified homoscedastic model

${\rm E}\big[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta\big]\simeq
\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}\,L\mu^{-2}$, $\qquad 
\mu^{2}= \pi^{\prime}Z^{\prime}Z\pi/\sigma_{v}^{2}$ ,

${\rm plim}\big[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta\big]=\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}$,
so that on the Nagar scale

$\rho_{N}(\mu^{2})\equiv
\frac{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]}
     {{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]}\simeq\frac{L}{\mu^{2}}$

and in large samples $F\simeq1+\mu^{2}/L$.  With $L=1$

$\rho_{N}\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq(F-1)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1}$,
i.e. the point Nagar rule $\rho_{N}\simeq0.10\iff\mu^{2}\simeq10\iff
F_{med}\simeq1+\mu^{2}\simeq 11$, the familiar $F\!\approx\!10$ rule.

In weak instrument asymptotics $kF\sim\chi^{2}_{k}(\mu^{2})$ and the
usual size/bias inversion is

${\rm P}\!\big\{\,F\ge F^{*} \mid \mu^{2}_{0}=L/0.10\,\big\}=0.95$,

i.e. the $5\%$ critical value of the non-central $F_{L,\infty}
(\mu^{2}_{0})$ with $\mu^{2}_{0}=L/0.10=10$.  For $k_{2}=L=1$ this is the
Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal relative-bias critical value

$F^{*}_{SY}=F_{0.95}\!\left(1,\mu^{2}_{0}=10\right)\approx16.38$,

i.e. $F^{*}\approx16\!-\!17$ on an integer scale, conventionally quoted
as $F\gtrsim16$, the $F>10$ point rule made $5\%$ size in the
Nagar/Stock–Yogo sense.  In particular $ {\rm E}[\rho_{N}]\simeq
1/(F-1)$ gives the point $1/F\approx0.10\iff F\approx10$, $F\approx11$
with the $F-1$ correction, and the $5\%$ size controlled maximal
relative-bias value is $F\approx16.4\approx16$.

*Remark.*  On the usual normal fiducial lower bound
$\sqrt F\dot\sim N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$,
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\simeq\sqrt F-z_{0.95}$ and
$\rho_{N,U}\simeq\big(\sqrt F-z_{0.95}\big)^{-2}$.
Putting $\rho_{N,U}=0.10$, $\mu^{2}_{L}=10$,

$\sqrt{F_{0.95}}=z_{0.95}+\sqrt{10}$,

so that with the one-sided $z_{0.95}=1.645$

$F_{0.95}\simeq\big(\sqrt{10}+1.645\big)^{2}\approx23.1\approx23\!-\!24$,

$F_{0.95}\simeq24$ on the $F-1\simeq\mu^{2}$ correction, and
$F_{0.95}^{2sd}\simeq\big(\sqrt{10}+1.96\big)^{2}\approx26.2\approx26$,
the familiar $F\approx10$ point Nagar rule inflated by the
$\sim1.6\!-\!2.0$ s.e. safety factor for the sampling variation of
$\sqrt F$.  This is the $20\!-\!30$ fiducial lower confidence bound for
$\mu^{2}>10$ often quoted as the $95\%$ confidence version of the
$F>10$ rule.

E[β̂2SLS-β]≈σ_uv/σ_v²·L/μ², plim OLS bias =σ_uv/σ_v², so

$F\simeq1+\mu^{2}/L$.  Pointwise $\rho_{N}=0.10$ is $\mu^{2}=L/0.10=10$,
i.e. $F-1\simeq10$, the familiar $F\simeq10\!-\!11$ rule.

Let $T=\sqrt F$.  In weak instrument asymptotics with homoscedastic
normal errors

$T\stackrel{a}{\sim}N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right)$,
$F\approx\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ ,
so up to the normal Taylor approximation a $1-\alpha$ lower fiducial
limit for the concentration parameter is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\simeq T-z_{1-\alpha},\qquad 
\mu^{2}_{L}\simeq\bigl(\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr)^{2}$,

and the $1-\alpha$ upper bound for the Nagar relative bias is

$\rho_{N}^{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}\simeq\bigl(\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr)^{-2}$ .

Putting $\rho_{N}^{U}=0.10$, i.e. $\mu^{2}_{L}=10$,

$\sqrt{F_{1-\alpha}}=z_{1-\alpha}+\sqrt{10}$ .

One sided $95\%$ normal $z_{0.95}=1.645$,

$\sqrt{F_{0.95}}\simeq3.162+1.645=4.81$,
$F_{0.95}\simeq( \sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\simeq23.1$,

i.e. an observed $F\approx22\!-\!24$ puts the $95\%$ one sided lower
fiducial limit for $\mu^{2}$ at $10$ and hence a $95\%$ upper limit
$\rho_{N}\lesssim0.10$.  With the usual small sample $\mu^{2}\simeq F-1$
correction this is $F\gtrsim24\!-\!25$.  On the conventional two sided
$z_{0.975}=1.96$ normalisation

$F_{0.95}^{2sd}\simeq(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\simeq26.2\approx26$,

the familiar $F\approx10$ point Nagar rule inflated by the $\approx
1.6\!-\!2.0$ s.e. safety factor for the first stage $t=\sqrt F$.

Remark.  The size controlled Stock–Yogo weak instrument inversion
${\rm P}\{F\ge F^{*}|\mu^{2}=10\}=0.95$, i.e. the $5\%$ test of
$H_{0}:\rho_{N}\ge0.10$, is $F^{*}_{SY}=16.38\approx16\!-\!17$, the
$F\approx16$ value usually quoted as the operational “$95\%$ confident
$10\%$ maximal relative bias’’ calibration.  This is the $1/F\approx0.10$
point rule made $5\%$ size controlled, as against the direct normal
fiducial lower confidence bound for $\mu^{2}$ quoted above.

12.text:
With $L=1$ first order homoscedastic Nagar

${\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]\approx \sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}\mu^{-2}$,
${\rm plim}{\rm Bias}_{OLS}=\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}$,

so that on the Nagar scale

$\rho_{N}(\mu^{2})\equiv {\rm RelBias}\approx L\mu^{-2}\approx\mu^{-2}$,

and in the weak instrument limit

$F\approx 1+\mu^{2},\qquad T:=\sqrt F\stackrel{a}{\sim}N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right)$.

Hence up to the $+1$ in $F\simeq1+\mu^{2}$

$\rho_{N}\approx F^{-1},\qquad 
\rho_{N}^{U,1-\alpha}\approx\Big[\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}\Big]^{-2}$,

the $1-\alpha$ upper bound being obtained from the $1-\alpha$ lower
fiducial bound $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\approx\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}$ for the
concentration parameter.  Putting $\rho_{N}^{U,1-\alpha}=0.10$ i.e.
$\mu^{2}_{L}=1/0.10=10$,

$\sqrt{F_{1-\alpha}}=z_{1-\alpha}+\sqrt{10}$ .

On the usual one-sided $95\%$ normalisation $z_{0.95}=1.645$,

$\sqrt{F_{0.95}}\approx\sqrt{10}+1.645\approx3.162+1.645=4.81$,
$F_{0.95}\approx\big(\sqrt{10}+1.645\big)^{2}\approx23.1$,

i.e. an observed first stage $F\approx22\!-\!24$ puts the $95\%$ one
sided lower fiducial limit for the concentration parameter at
$\mu^{2}_{L}\approx10$ and hence a $95\%$ upper bound
$\rho_{N,0.95}\approx\mu_{L}^{-2}\approx0.10$ for the Nagar relative bias.
With the textbook $\mu^{2}\simeq F-1$ small sample correction this is
$F-1\gtrsim(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}$ i.e. $F\gtrsim24\!-\!25$ in practice,
$F\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26.2\approx26$ on the conventional
two sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ normalisation.

The median point Nagar rule is of course $\rho_{N}\approx1/F\approx0.10\iff
F\approx10$, $F-1\approx10\iff F\approx11$.  Inverting the non-central
$\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ exactly, i.e. the Stock–Yogo maximal relative bias
$5\%$ size test $P\big[F\ge F^{*}|\mu^{2}=L/0.10=10\big]=0.95$, gives the
conventional operational weak instrument critical value

$F^{*}_{SY}\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

commonly quoted as $F\gtrsim16$, the $F>10$ point Nagar rule made $5\%$
size / $95\%$ confidence in the Stock–Yogo sense.  This is the $F\approx16$
value usually reported in the literature; the $F\approx23\!-\!26$ number
above is the direct $95\%$ lower confidence bound for $\mu^{2}$ obtained
from the normal $\sqrt F\sim N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ fiducial approximation.

2.text:
With $L=1$ under homoscedasticity the Nagar first order relative bias is

${\rm RelBias}_{N}\simeq L/\mu^{2}\simeq 1/\mu^{2}$ , 
$\qquad \mu^{2}= \pi^{\prime}Z^{\prime}Z\pi/\sigma_{v}^{2}$ , 

and in large samples $F\simeq 1+\mu^{2}/L$, so that on the mean scale

${\rm RelBias}_{N}\simeq 1/(F-1)\simeq 1/F$
and the point Nagar $10\%$ rule is $\mu^{2}=10$, $F_{med}\simeq1+\mu^{2}\simeq
11$, the familiar $F\approx10$ rule.

In the weak instrument limit $T=\sqrt F\stackrel{a}{\sim}
N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ so that up to the $F-1$ correction a $1-\alpha$ 
one sided fiducial lower bound for the concentration parameter is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\simeq\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha},
\qquad 
\mu^{2}_{L}\simeq\bigl(\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr)^{2}$ ,

and a $1-\alpha$ upper bound for the Nagar relative bias is
$\rho_{N}^{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}\simeq(\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha})^{-2}$.
Putting $\rho_{N}^{U}=0.10$, i.e. $\mu_{L}^{2}=1/0.10=10$,

$\sqrt{F_{1-\alpha}}=z_{1-\alpha}+\sqrt{10}$ .

With the one sided $95\%$ normal quantile $z_{0.95}=1.645$

$\sqrt{F_{0.95}}\simeq\sqrt{10}+1.645\simeq3.162+1.645=4.81$

so that on the $F\simeq1+\mu^{2}$ scale

$F_{0.95}\simeq\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\simeq23.1\approx23$,

i.e. $F-1\gtrsim(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}$ or $F\gtrsim24\!-\!25$ on the
usual $ \mu^{2}\simeq F-1$ small sample correction.  With the
conventional two sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ this is
$F\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26$ , the familiar $F\approx20\!-\!30$
$95\%$ lower fiducial bound for $\mu^{2}>10$.

Remark.  The size controlled Stock–Yogo inversion
${\rm P}\{F\ge F^{*}\mid\mu^{2}_{0}=L/0.10=10\}=0.95$ is the usual
operational weak instrument calibration.  For $k_{2}=L=1$ this is the
$10\%$ maximal relative bias $5\%$ critical value

$F^{*}_{SY}=F_{0.95}\!\left(1,\mu^{2}_{0}=10\right)\approx16.38\approx
16\!-\!17$,

i.e. $F\approx16$ on the Stock–Yogo maximal-relative-bias scale, the
conventional $F>10$ rule made $5\%$ size.  This is the $ \approx 16.4$ value
usually quoted as the $95\%$ confidence, $10\%$ maximal Nagar bias
threshold, as against the $\approx23\!-\!26$ normal fiducial lower bound
for $\mu^{2}$ quoted above.

10.text:
In the homoskedastic just identified case

${\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]\simeq \sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}\,
L\mu^{-2},\qquad L=1,$

so on the Nagar scale with ${\rm plim}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]=\sigma_{uv}
\sigma_{v}^{-2}$

$\rho_{N}(\mu^{2})\simeq L\mu^{-2}\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq
(F-1)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1}$ ,    $F\simeq1+\mu^{2}/L$ ,

and $\rho_{N}=0.10$ in the mean is $\mu^{2}=L/0.10=10$, $F_{med}\simeq
1+10\simeq11$, the familiar $F\approx10$ rule.

Put $T=\sqrt F$.  In weak instrument asymptotics with normal errors

$T\stackrel{a}{\sim}N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right),\qquad 
F\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2}) ,$

so that to first order a $1-\alpha$ one-sided fiducial lower bound for
the concentration parameter is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\simeq T-z_{1-\alpha},\qquad
\mu^{2}_{L}\simeq\bigl(\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr)^{2},$

and

$\rho_{N}^{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}\simeq
\bigl(\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr)^{-2}$

is a $1-\alpha$ upper bound for the Nagar relative bias.  Putting
$\rho_{N}^{U}=0.10$, i.e. $\mu_{L}^{2}=10$,

$\sqrt{F_{1-\alpha}}=z_{1-\alpha}+\sqrt{10}.$

With the one-sided $95\%$ normal quantile $z_{0.95}=1.645$

$\sqrt{F_{0.95}}\simeq 3.162+1.645=4.81,$

$F_{0.95}\simeq\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\simeq23.1,$

i.e. $F\approx22\!-\!24$ on the $F\simeq1+\mu^{2}$ scale.  On the usual
small sample $\mu^{2}\simeq F-1$ scale

$F-1\simeq\bigl(\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}\bigr)^{2}$,

$F_{0.95}^{F-1}\simeq1+\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\simeq24.1\approx24$,
and with the conventional two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$,

$F_{0.95}^{2sd}\simeq\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.96\bigr)^{2}\simeq26.2\approx26$,

the familiar $F\approx10$ point Nagar rule inflated by the $\sim1.6\!-\!2.0$
s.e. safety factor for the sampling variation of $\sqrt F$.

Up to the $F-1$ correction this is the $F\approx 20\!-\!30$ $95\%$ lower
confidence bound for $\mu^{2}>10$, about $F\approx23$ uncorrected,
$F\approx24$ with the $F-1\simeq\mu^{2}$ correction.  This is the direct
$95\%$ lower confidence bound for the concentration parameter,
$\mu^{2}_{L}>10\Leftrightarrow\rho_{N}<0.10$.

Remark.  The operational Stock–Yogo maximal-relative-bias calibration
inverts $P\!\left[F>F^{*}\mid\mu^{2}=L/0.10\right]=0.05$ under
$kF\sim\chi^{2}_{k}(\mu^{2})$.  For $k=L=1,\;\mu_{0}^{2}=10$ this is

$F^{*}_{SY}=F_{0.05}\!\left(1,\infty;\mu^{2}=10\right)\simeq16.38\approx16\!-\!17,$

the value usually quoted as the $10\%$ maximal relative bias $5\%$
size threshold, i.e. the $F>10$ rule made $95\%$ confident in the
Stock–Yogo size-control sense.  With the $F-1$ correction
$\rho_{N}\simeq1/(F-1)$ this is $\rho_{N}\approx0.067$ at $F\approx16$.
∎

8.text:
For the just-identified homoscedastic model with $L=1$

${\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]\simeq \sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}\mu^{-2}$ ,
${\rm plim}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]=\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}$,

so that on the Nagar scale

$\rho_{N}(\mu^{2})\equiv
\frac{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]}{{\rm plim}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]}
\simeq L\mu^{-2}\simeq\mu^{-2}$ ,

and in the weak instrument limit

$F =\frac{\hat\pi^{2}\sum z^{2}}{\hat\sigma_{v}^{2}}\approx 1+\mu^{2}$ ,
$T:=\sqrt F\stackrel{a}{\sim}N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right) $,
$F\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ .

Up to the $1$ in $F\simeq1+\mu^{2}$

$\rho_{N}\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq F^{-1}$ .

Put $T\sim N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$.  A $1-\alpha$ lower fiducial bound for
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\simeq T-z_{1-\alpha}=\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}$ ,

so that a $1-\alpha$ upper bound for the Nagar relative bias is

$\rho_{N}^{U}\simeq \mu_{L}^{-2}\simeq\bigl[\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr]^{-2}$ .

Put $\rho_{N}^{U}=0.10$, i.e. $\mu_{L}^{2}=1/0.10=10$,

$\sqrt{F_{1-\alpha}}-z_{1-\alpha}=\sqrt{10}$ ,
$\sqrt{F_{1-\alpha}}=z_{1-\alpha}+\sqrt{10}$ .

With the one sided $95\%$ normal quantile $z_{0.95}=1.645$

$\sqrt{F_{0.95}}\simeq 1.645+3.162=4.807$,

$F_{0.95}\simeq( \sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx 23.1$,

i.e. an observed first stage $F\approx23\!-\!24$ puts the $95\%$ one-sided
lower fiducial limit for the concentration parameter at $\mu^{2}_{L}=10$
and hence the $95\%$ upper limit for the Nagar relative bias at
$\rho_{N}^{U}\approx0.10$.  On the usual small sample
$\mu^{2}\simeq F-1$ scale this is $F-1\gtrsim(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}$,
$F\gtrsim24$, and with the conventional two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$

$F_{0.95}^{2sd}\simeq(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26.2$,

the familiar $F\approx10$ point Nagar rule $ \rho_{N}\approx1/F$ inflated
by the $\approx1.6\!-\!2.0$ s.e. safety factor for the first stage
$t=\sqrt F$.  The median point Nagar rule is $1/F=0.10\iff F\approx10$,
$F-1\approx10\iff F\approx11$, the $F>10$ rule.

Remark.  Inverting the exact non-central $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ law,
$P\{F>F^{*}|\mu^{2}=10\}=0.05$, i.e. the Stock–Yogo maximal-relative-bias
$5\%$ size calibration, gives the conventional operational threshold

$F^{*}_{SY}\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

the $F\approx10$ point estimate made $95\%$ confident in the
Stock–Yogo maximal-bias sense.  This is the $F\approx16$ value quoted in
the weak-instrument tables and is the normal-approximation $23\!-\!24$
bound without the $z$ safety factor.

public_text.14:
The Nagar first order relative bias for the just identified homoscedastic case is

ρ_N ≃ L/μ² ,    L=1 ,      μ² = π′Z′Zπ/σ_v²

and plim β̂_OLS-β = σ_uv/σ_v² , so that

ρ_N ≃ 1/μ² ≃ 1/(F-1) ≃ 1/F

with F≈1+μ² in large samples. Pointwise ρ_N =0.10 is μ²=10 i.e. F≈11, the familiar F>10 rule.

The 95% confidence statement about that bias is the Stock–Yogo weak-instrument inversion. Under weak instrument asymptotics with homoscedastic normal errors

k₂F →ᵈ χ²_{k₂}(μ²),   k₂=1

and ρ_N is monotone decreasing in μ². The operational 5% test of

H0 : maximal relative bias ≥0.10  ⇔  μ²₀ = L/0.10 =10

vs H1 : maximal relative bias <0.10 is

P[ F ≥ F* | μ²=μ²₀ ] =0.95

i.e. F* is the 5% left tail of the non-central F_{1,∞}(μ²₀=10). Inverting the non-central χ²₁(10) gives

F* = F_{0.95}(1, μ²=10) ≃ 16.38

≈16–17 on the integer scale, the value tabulated by Stock–Yogo for the 10% maximal relative bias, 5% size test with k₂=1, L=1. With F_obs≈16 the Nagar point estimate is ρ_N≈1/(F-1)≈0.067<0.10 and the 5% size maximal bias test is satisfied.

The √F≈N(√μ²,1) fiducial bound √μ²_L≈√F−z_{1-α} and μ²_L≈(√F−z)² that gives √F_{0.95}=√10+z_{0.95} and F≈(√10+1.645)²≈23.1 is a normal delta-method lower bound for √μ². It treats the √F normal approximation as exact, replaces μ² by F rather than F-1 and uses a fiducial lower confidence limit for the concentration parameter itself rather than the non-central χ² inversion that defines the Nagar/Stock–Yogo maximal relative bias test. The normal approximation to √F is only first order accurate for large μ² and is markedly skewed at μ²=10, whence the √(F) bound double counts sampling variation and the +1 in F≈1+μ². That is why it inflates the tabulated Stock–Yogo critical value from ≈16.4 to ≈23–26.

In the literature the operational 95% confidence implementation of “the Nagar relative bias is <10%” is therefore the Stock–Yogo maximal relative bias critical value, F*≈16.38, i.e. ≈16 to the nearest whole number, the familiar F>10 rule made 95% confident in the Nagar/Stock–Yogo sense.
public_text.7:
The Nagar first order relative bias with L=1 is 

RelBias_N ≈ 1/μ² ≈ 1/(F-1) ≈ 1/F

in the just identified homoscedastic case, with μ² = π′Z′Zπ/σ_v² and plim F = 1+μ².

In weak instrument asymptotics

T := √F  ↝ N(√μ²,1) ,   F ↝ χ²₁(μ²)

so that a fiducial lower bound for the concentration parameter is

√μ²_L ≈ √F - z_{1-α} ,    μ²_L ≈ (√F - z_{1-α})² .

The 1-α upper bound for the Nagar relative bias is therefore

ρ_{N,U} ≈ 1 / (√F - z_{1-α})² .

Putting ρ_{N,U}=0.10 i.e. μ²_L = 1/0.10 =10 gives the familiar inversion

√F_{1-α}= z_{1-α}+√10 .

Now the 95% confidence statement for μ² is usually taken as a conventional two-sided 95% normal interval for T.  A two-sided 95% interval for a normal mean is ±z_{0.975}=1.96, i.e. the one-sided lower 2.5% quantile.  The one-sided z_{0.95}=1.645 quantile is the 90% two-sided normal interval and is not the conventional 95% confidence bound that is quoted for √F.

With the conventional two-sided 95% normal quantile

√F_{0.95}^{2sd}= 1.96 + √10 ≈ 1.96 + 3.162 =5.122

so that

F_{0.95}^{2sd}≈ (√10+1.96)²≈26.2≈26

on the √F normal approximation.  On the μ²≈F-1 scale this is 
F-1≈(√10+1.96)² i.e. F≈27 in practice, the 25-27 range often quoted as the 95% confident version of the F≈10 point rule.

The one-sided value √F≈√10+1.645≈4.81, F≈23.1, is the 95% one-sided / 90% two-sided normal bound for √μ².  Textbooks and the usual confidence reporting use z_{0.975}=1.96 for a 95% two-sided confidence statement, which is the 1.6–2.0 s.e. safety factor normally applied to the first-stage t=√F.  That is the 20-30 rule that is the operational 95% confidence implementation of the Nagar 10% relative bias condition in the √F≈N(√μ²,1) approximation.

The Stock–Yogo value F*≈16.38 is the 5% size critical value of the non-central F for a maximal relative bias test, i.e. a size-control inversion P(F>F*|μ²=10)=0.05, not the fiducial 95% lower confidence bound μ²_L≥10 for the concentration parameter obtained from √F≈N(√μ²,1).  The point 1/F≈0.10 ⇔ F≈10 is the mean relation; the confidence bound for μ² is the (√10+z)² inversion above, ≈26 with the conventional two-sided 95% normal quantile, ≈23-24 on the one-sided 1.645 convention.

E[β̂2SLS-β] ≈ σuv/σv² · L/μ² ,   μ² = π′Z′Zπ/σv²

so that relative to OLS

ρN ≈ L/μ² ≈ 1/μ² ≈ 1/(F-1) ≈ 1/F

in the just identified limit, F ≈ 1+ μ²/L.  Pointwise ρN=0.10 is μ² = L/0.10 =10, i.e. E[F]≈11, the familiar F≈10 rule.

The 95% confidence statement “ρN<0.10 with 95% confidence” is the weak-instrument size calibration. Under weak-instrument asymptotics

k2F →d χ²k2(μ²)

and ρN is monotone decreasing in μ².  The operational test is

P[ F ≥ Fobs | μ²0 = L/0.10 ] =0.95

i.e. the 5% critical value of the first-stage F under the null maximal relative bias =0.10.  With L=k2=1, μ²0=10, the inversion of the non-central χ²1(10) is the Stock-Yogo maximal relative bias 10% critical value

F* = F0.95(1,∞; μ²=10) ≈ 16.38

≈16 on an integer scale, conventionally quoted as F≈16–17.

On the textbook Nagar/Stock-Yogo calibration the 10% maximal relative bias 5% test is therefore F*≈16.38, i.e. ≈16 to the nearest whole number, the F>10 rule made 95% confident in the weak-instrument literature.
public_text.5:
With a single instrument the first-order Nagar bias is

E[β̂2SLS-β] ≈ σuv/σv² · L/μ² ,  L=1 ,

so on the Nagar scale

ρN ≈ L/μ² ≈ 1/μ² .

The point rule ρN=0.10 is therefore μ²= L/0.10 =10, i.e. F-1≈10 or the familiar F≈10-11 rule of thumb.

and ρN is monotone decreasing in μ².  The conventional operationalisation is

P[ F ≥ F* | μ² = L/0.10 ] =0.95 ,

i.e. the 5% left tail of the non-central first stage under the null maximal relative bias μ²0 =10.  That is the Stock–Yogo maximal relative bias test.

For k2 = L =1

F* = F0.95(k=1, μ²0=10) ≈ 16.38

is the 5% critical value of the non-central χ²1(10).  With Fobs ≥ F* we have

It double-counts sampling variation, replaces the non-central χ² law by a normal approximation to √F and ignores the F-1 non-linearity.  It is a conservative safety factor for √μ², not the Stock–Yogo inversion P(F≥f|μ²=10)=0.95 that the weak instrument literature uses to define “95% confidence that the Nagar relative bias is <10% of the OLS bias”.  That is why the literature quotes the operational 10% maximal relative bias threshold as F*≈16.4, i.e. ≈16.
public_text.13:
The Nagar first order expression that is normally used for this question is

E[ β̂2SLS - β ] ≃ σuv/σv² · L/μ² ,    μ² = π′Z′Zπ/σv² ,

plim[β̂OLS-β]=σuv/σv² so that on the Nagar scale

ρN ≡ Bias2SLS / BiasOLS ≃ L/μ² .

With L=1 and k2=1, F ≃ 1+μ² and to first order ρN ≃ 1/(F-1) ≃ 1/F. The point Nagar rule ρN≈0.10 is F≈10, F-1≈10.

The 95% confidence statement about that asymptotic relative bias is the Stock-Yogo weak instrument calibration, i.e. the inversion of the first stage distribution under a given concentration parameter. Under homoscedastic normal errors

k2 F → χ²k2(μ²)

and the Nagar relative bias is monotone decreasing in μ². The 5% test of

H0 : maximal relative bias ≥0.10  ⇔  μ²0 = L/0.10 =10

vs H1 : maximal relative bias <0.10 is

P[ F ≥ F* | μ² = 10 ] =0.95 .

That is exactly the conventional “95% confident that the Nagar relative bias is <10%” statement used in the weak instrument literature. It is not a fiducial lower bound for √μ² and it is not the normal delta method bound μ²L=(√F−z)².

For k2=L=1 the inversion of the non-central χ²₁(10), i.e. the non-central F1,∞(10), is

F* = F0.95(1,∞; μ²0=10) ≈ 16.38 .

Hence with the usual F-1≈μ² small sample correction the point estimate 1/(F-1)=0.10 is F≈11 and the 5% size maximal relative bias calibration lifts it to F*≈16.4. In practice this is quoted as the F>10 rule made 95% confident, conventionally F≈16-17, ≈16 to the nearest whole number.

The √F≃N(√μ²,1) bound √μ²L≈√F−z0.95 → μ²L≈(√F−z)² → F≈(√10+z0.95)²≈23 is a normal fiducial lower bound for the concentration parameter itself. It treats √F as exactly normal with unit variance, squares the bound and therefore double counts the sampling variation of the non-linear transform μ²=(√F−z)², and it is not the non-central F inversion that defines the Stock-Yogo maximal relative bias test. That normal approximation is conservative and is not the operational definition of “95% confidence that the relative asymptotic bias is <10%” used in the Nagar/Stock-Yogo literature. The textbook operational threshold is the Stock-Yogo 10% maximal relative bias critical value, F*≈16.38≈16.

With one instrument, homoscedastic errors and just identification the Nagar first order relative bias is the object the weak instrument literature operationalises,

E[β̂2SLS−β] ≃ σuv/σv² · L/μ² ,   μ² = π′Z′Zπ/σv² ,

plim β̂OLS−β = σuv/σv²,  L=1,

so that on the Nagar scale

ρN ≃ L/μ² ≃ 1/μ² ≃ 1/(F−1) ≃ 1/F

in large samples, F ≃ 1+μ²/L. Pointwise ρN=0.10 is μ²=10, i.e. F≈11, the familiar F≈10 rule.

The operational 95% confidence statement about that bias is the Stock-Yogo maximal relative bias calibration. Under weak instrument asymptotics k2F →d χ²k2(μ²) and the Nagar bias is monotone decreasing in μ². The conventional test is

P[ F ≥ F* | μ² = μ0² ] = 0.95 ,     μ0² = L/0.10 , 

i.e. the 5% left tail of the non-central F under the null that the maximal relative bias is 10%. Inverting the non-central distribution is the definition of “95% confident that the Nagar relative bias is <10%” used in the weak instrument literature.

For k2 = L =1, μ0² = 1/0.10 =10, the 5% Stock-Yogo critical value is

F* = F0.95(1,μ²0=10) ≈ 16.38,

i.e. ≈16–17 on an integer scale, conventionally quoted as F≈16. With F≈16 the Nagar point estimate is ρN≈1/(F−1)≈0.067<0.10 and the maximal relative bias test is satisfied at the 5% level. This is the F>10 rule made 95% confident in the Nagar/Stock-Yogo sense.

The √F≈N(√μ²,1) bound √μ²L≈√F−z1−α with μ²L>10,

√F1−α = z1−α+√10,  F1−α≈(√10+z0.95)²≈23.1,

is a delta-method fiducial lower bound for the concentration parameter μ² itself. It treats the bound on √μ² as a bound on μ² and then plugs μ²L into 1/μ², i.e. it is a normal approximation to a lower confidence limit for μ², not the non-central χ² inversion that defines the Stock-Yogo maximal relative bias test. It uses the large μ² normal approximation to √F in a region μ²≈10 where the non-central χ²1 is visibly skewed, it double counts the +1 in F≈1+μ², and it is the source of the 22–26 numbers. With the F−1 correction it becomes even more conservative, F≳24–26 with z0.975.

The textbook operationalisation of “95% confidence that the relative asymptotic Nagar bias is <10% of the OLS bias” is therefore the Stock-Yogo 10% maximal relative bias critical value, F*≈16.38, essentially F≈16 to the nearest whole number, the usual F>10 rule made 95% confident.

The first order Nagar bias under homoskedasticity with $L=1$ is

$${\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]\simeq \frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{v}^{2}}\frac{1}{\mu^{2}},\qquad 
{\rm plim}\big[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta\big]=\frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{v}^{2}}, $$

so that on the Nagar scale

$$\rho_{N}(\mu^{2})\equiv
\frac{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]}
     {{\rm plim}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]}\simeq\frac1{\mu^{2}} ,
\qquad 
F\approx 1+\mu^{2}
 $$

and on the population scale $\rho_{N}\approx 1/(F-1)\approx1/F$.
Pointwise $\rho_{N}=0.10$ is $\mu^{2}=10$, i.e. $F\approx1+\mu^{2}\approx11$,
the familiar $F\simeq10$ rule.

In the weak instrument limit with $k_{2}=1$

$$T:=\sqrt{F}\;\stackrel{a}{\sim}\;N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right),\qquad 
F\approx\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2}), $$

so a one sided $1-\alpha$ fiducial lower bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is

$$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\simeq\sqrt{F_{obs}}-z_{1-\alpha},\qquad 
\mu^{2}_{L}\simeq\Bigl(\sqrt{F_{obs}}-z_{1-\alpha}\Bigr)^{2}, $$

and a $1-\alpha$ upper bound for the Nagar relative bias is
$\rho_{N}^{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}\simeq\bigl(\sqrt{F}-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr)^{-2}$.
Putting $\rho_{N}^{U}=0.10$, i.e. $\mu^{2}_{L}=10$,

$$\sqrt{F_{1-\alpha}}=z_{1-\alpha}+\sqrt{10}\;.$$

With the usual one sided $95\%$ normal quantile $z_{0.95}=1.645$

$$\sqrt{F_{0.95}}\simeq\sqrt{10}+1.645\simeq3.162+1.645=4.807,$$

$$F_{0.95}\simeq\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\simeq23.1, $$

i.e. an observed $F\approx23\!-\!24$ puts the $95\%$ lower fiducial limit
$\mu^{2}_{L}\approx10$ on the concentration parameter and hence a $95\%$
upper limit $\rho_{N}\lesssim0.10$ on the Nagar relative bias.  On the
conventional $\mu^{2}\simeq F-1$ small sample correction this is
$F-1\gtrsim(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}$, $F\gtrsim24\!-\!25$, and with the
text-book two sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ quantile
$F_{0.95}^{2sd}\simeq(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\simeq26.2\approx26$.
The median point Nagar rule is of course $1/F\approx0.10\iff F\approx10$,
$F-1\approx10$.

Remark.  The size controlled Stock–Yogo inversion of the non-central
$F$,
${\rm P}\{F\ge F^{*}|\mu^{2}=L/0.10=10\}=0.95$, gives the conventional
tabulated $10\%$ maximal relative bias $5\%$ critical value
$F^{*}_{SY}\simeq16.38\approx16\!-\!17$, the $F>10$ rule made $95\%$
confident in the usual weak-instrument operational sense.

With Fobs ≥16.38 we have P[ μ²≥10 | Fobs ]≈0.95 and hence P[ ρN =1/μ² ≤0.10 | Fobs ]≈0.95 in the Nagar/Stock–Yogo sense. On the usual μ²≃F-1 scale this gives the point estimate ρN≃1/(F-1)≈0.067 at F=16, <0.10.

The √F≈N(√μ²,1) bound √μ²L≃√F−z1-α, μ²L≃(√F−z1-α)², which gives √F1-α=z1-α+√10 and F1-α≈(√10+1.645)²≈23.1, ≈24–26 with the F-1 correction and two-sided z=1.96, is a normal delta-method lower fiducial bound for the concentration parameter itself. It treats the √F normal approximation as exact at μ²=10 where the non-central χ²₁ is markedly skewed, it squares a bound for √μ² and therefore double counts sampling variation, and it replaces the non-central F inversion P[F≥f|μ²=10]=0.95 that defines the maximal bias test by a normal approximation to √F. That is why the number moves from ≈23 to ≈24–26 with the F-1 correction and with one- vs two-sided z, and why it is conservative relative to the tabulated Stock–Yogo critical value.

In the weak instrument literature the textbook operationalisation of “95% confident that the asymptotic Nagar relative bias is <10% of the OLS bias” with k2=L=1 is the Stock–Yogo 10% maximal relative bias 5% size critical value, F*≈16.38, i.e. ≈16 to the nearest whole number, the conventional F>10 rule made 95% confident.

2.text:
With $L=1$ the homoscedastic Nagar first order relative bias on the OLS
scale is

${\rm RelBias}_{N}\simeq L/\mu^{2}\simeq 1/\mu^{2}\simeq1/(F-1)\simeq 1/F$,
$\qquad F\simeq 1+\mu^{2}$, 

so that on the mean scale ${\rm RelBias}_{N}=0.10$ is the point Nagar
rule

$\mu^{2}_{0}=L/0.10=10\iff F_{med}\simeq1+\mu^{2}_{0}\simeq11$,
the familiar $F\approx10$ rule.

In weak instrument asymptotics

$k_{2}F\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\chi^{2}_{k_{2}}(\mu^{2}),\qquad k_{2}=1$,

and ${\rm RelBias}_{N}$ is monotone decreasing in $\mu^{2}$.  The
operational $5\%$ size test of the Nagar maximal relative bias

$H_{0}:\;{\rm RelBias}_{N}\ge0.10\iff \mu^{2}\le\mu^{2}_{0}=L/0.10=10$

against $H_{1}:{\rm RelBias}_{N}<0.10$ is therefore

${\rm P}\!\left\{F\ge F^{*}\mid\mu^{2}=\mu^{2}_{0}=10\right\}=0.95$,

i.e. the $5\%$ left tail of the non-central first stage under the null
maximal relative bias.  For $k_{2}=L=1$

$F^{*}=F_{0.95}\bigl(1,\infty;\mu^{2}=10\bigr)$

is the Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal relative bias $5\%$ size critical
value.  Inverting the non-central $\chi^{2}_{1}(10)$,

$F^{*}_{SY}\simeq16.38$,

so that $F_{obs}\ge F^{*}$ gives ${\rm P}\{\mu^{2}\ge10\mid F_{obs}\}
\approx0.95$ and ${\rm RelBias}_{N}\approx1/(F-1)\lesssim0.10$ at the
$5\%$ size.  On an integer scale this is the usual $F\approx16\!-\!17$
operational rule, $F\approx16$ to the nearest whole number, the $F>10$
point Nagar rule made $95\%$ confident in the Stock–Yogo maximal
bias sense.  With the $F-1\simeq\mu^{2}$ correction
${\rm RelBias}_{N}\approx1/(F-1)\approx0.067$ at $F\approx16$.

Remark.  On the $\sqrt F\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ fiducial
normalisation the $1-\alpha$ lower bound for the concentration parameter
is $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\simeq\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}$,
$\mu^{2}_{L}\simeq(\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha})^{2}$.  Putting
$\mu^{2}_{L}=10$ gives $\sqrt{F_{1-\alpha}}=z_{1-\alpha}+\sqrt{10}$, i.e.
$F_{0.95}\simeq(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\simeq23.1$, $F\simeq24$ on the
$F-1\simeq\mu^{2}$ scale and $F\simeq(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\simeq26.2$
with the conventional two sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$.  This is the direct
$95\%$ lower fiducial confidence bound for $\mu^{2}>10$, the
$F\approx20\!-\!30$ safety factor often quoted alongside the
Stock–Yogo size-controlled $F^{*}\approx16.4$ threshold. ∎

4.text:
With $L=1$ the first order homoskedastic Nagar bias on the OLS scale is

${\rm E}[\hat \beta_{2SLS}-\beta]\simeq\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}L\mu^{-2}$,
${\rm plim}[\hat \beta_{OLS}-\beta]=\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}$,

so that on the Nagar scale

$\rho_{N}(\mu^{2})\equiv
{\rm Bias}_{2SLS}/{\rm Bias}_{OLS}\simeq L\mu^{-2}
\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq (F-1)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1}$,

$F\simeq 1+\mu^{2}/L$ in large samples.  Pointwise

$\rho_{N}=0.10\iff \mu^{2}=L/0.10=10\iff F-1\simeq10$,

i.e. the familiar $F\simeq10$-$11$ mean Nagar rule.

The weak-instrument operationalisation of “$95\%$ confident that
$\rho_{N}<0.10$’’ is the usual size controlled inversion

${\rm P}\!\left\{F\ge F^{*} \mid \mu^{2}_{0}=L/0.10\right\}=0.95$,

i.e. the $5\%$ test of $H_{0}:\rho_{N}\ge0.10\iff\mu^{2}\le10$ vs
$H_{1}:\rho_{N}<0.10$.  Under weak instrument asymptotics

$k_{2}F\stackrel{d}{\to}\chi^{2}_{k_{2}}(\mu^{2}),\qquad k_{2}=1$,

and $\rho_{N}$ is monotone decreasing in $\mu^{2}$.  For $k_{2}=L=1$
and $\mu^{2}_{0}=10$

$F^{*}=F_{0.95}\!\left(1,\infty;\mu^{2}=10\right)$

is the Stock-Yogo $10\%$ maximal relative bias $5\%$ size critical value.
Inverting the non-central $\chi^{2}_{1}(10)$,

$F^{*}_{SY}\simeq16.38\approx16\text{--}17$,

conventionally quoted as $F\gtrsim16$, the $F>10$ point Nagar rule made
$5\%$ size/$95\%$ confident in the Nagar/Stock-Yogo sense.  On the
$F-1\simeq\mu^{2}$ scale this is $\rho_{N}\simeq1/(F-1)\simeq0.067<0.10$
at $F\simeq16$.

Remark on the fiducial $\sqrt F$ bound.  With $T=\sqrt F$, 
$T\stackrel{a}{\sim}N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ and a $1-\alpha$ one-sided
fiducial lower bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is 
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\simeq\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}$,
$\mu^{2}_{L}\simeq(\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha})^{2}$,
$\rho_{N}^{U}\simeq(\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha})^{-2}$.
Putting $\rho_{N}^{U}=0.10$ i.e. $\mu^{2}_{L}=10$,

$\sqrt{F_{1-\alpha}}=z_{1-\alpha}+\sqrt{10}$,

so that one-sided $z_{0.95}=1.645$

$F_{0.95}\simeq(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\simeq23.1$,

$F-1\gtrsim23.1\iff F\gtrsim24.1\approx24\text{--}25$ on the usual
$\mu^{2}\simeq F-1$ correction, and with the conventional two-sided
$z_{0.975}=1.96$

$F_{0.95}^{2sd}\simeq(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\simeq26.2\approx26$,

the $\sqrt F\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ normal fiducial $95\%$ lower
bound for the concentration parameter, i.e. the $\approx 20$-$30$ 
safety-factor version of the $F>10$ rule.  The $F^{*}\simeq16.4$ value
above is the non-central-$F$ inversion that is quoted in the
weak-instrument literature as the operational $95\%$ confident $10\%$
maximal relative bias threshold. ∎

3.text:
With $L=k_{2}=1$ the homoskedastic first order Nagar relative bias on the
OLS scale is

${\rm RelBias}_{N}\simeq\frac{L}{\mu^{2}}\simeq\mu^{-2}
\simeq (F-1)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1} ,\qquad 
F\simeq1+\mu^{2},$

${\rm plim}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]=\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}$ and
${\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]\simeq\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}\,
L\mu^{-2}$.
Pointwise
${\rm RelBias}_{N}=0.10\iff \mu^{2}=L/0.10=10\iff F_{med}\simeq1+10\simeq
11$, the familiar $F\approx10$ rule.

Let $k_{2}F\to_{d}\chi^{2}_{k_{2}}(\mu^{2})$ in the weak instrument
limit.  ${\rm RelBias}_{N}$ is monotone decreasing in $\mu^{2}$ so that a
$1-\alpha$ lower confidence bound for $\mu^{2}$ is obtained by the
non-central inversion

${\rm P}\!\left\{F\ge F_{obs}\mid \mu^{2}=\mu_{L}^{2}\right\}= \alpha$,
i.e.  ${\rm P}\{F\ge F^{*}\mid\mu^{2}_{0}\}=1-\alpha$ for the $5\%$ size
test of $H_{0}:{\rm RelBias}_{N}\ge0.10\iff\mu^{2}_{0}=L/0.10$.
Hence

${\rm P}\!\left\{F\ge F^{*}\mid\mu^{2}_{0}=10\right\}=0.95$,

the usual Stock--Yogo maximal relative bias calibration.  For $k_{2}=L=1$

$F^{*}=F_{0.95}\bigl(1,\infty;\mu^{2}=10\bigr)$

is the $95{\rm th}$ percentile of a non-central $\chi^{2}_{1}(10)$,
$F^{*}\simeq16.38$.  With $F_{obs}\ge F^{*}$

${\rm P}\{\mu^{2}\ge10\mid F_{obs}\}\simeq0.95$ and
${\rm P}\{{\rm RelBias}_{N}=1/\mu^{2}\le0.10\mid F_{obs}\}\simeq0.95$
in the Nagar/Stock–Yogo sense.  On the $F-1\simeq\mu^{2}$ scale
${\rm RelBias}_{N}\simeq1/(F-1)\simeq0.067$ at $F^{*}$.  This is the
text-book operational $10\%$ maximal relative bias $5\%$ size threshold,
commonly quoted as $F\approx16\!-\!17$, $\approx16$ to the nearest
integer, i.e. the $F>10$ rule made $95\%$ confident.

Remark.  On the normal delta method approximation $T=\sqrt{F}\stackrel{a}
{\sim}N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ a $1-\alpha$ fiducial lower bound for the
concentration parameter is $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\simeq\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}$,
$\mu^{2}_{L}\simeq(\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha})^{2}$ and
$\rho_{N}^{U}\simeq(\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha})^{-2}$.
Putting $\rho_{N}^{U}=0.10$, $\mu_{L}^{2}=10$,

$\sqrt{F_{1-\alpha}}=z_{1-\alpha}+\sqrt{10}$,

so that with the one-sided $z_{0.95}=1.645$,
$F_{0.95}\simeq(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\simeq23.1$, $\simeq24\!-\!25$ on the
$F-1$ scale, and with the conventional two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$
$F_{0.95}^{2sd}\simeq(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\simeq26.2\approx26$, the
familiar $F\approx20\!-\!30$ normal fiducial safety factor for
$\mu^{2}_{L}\ge10$.  The $16.4$ Stock–Yogo value is the exact
non-central-$\chi^{2}$ inversion of that statement.

12.text:
With one endogenous regressor and one instrument under
homoscedasticity

E[β̂2SLS-β] ≃ σuv/σv² L/μ² ,   plim[β̂OLS-β]=σuv/σv² ,

ρN(μ²)=E[β̂2SLS-β]/plim[β̂OLS-β] ≃ L/μ² , L=1,

and in the weak instrument limit

F ≃ 1+μ²/L ,    ρN ≃ L/μ² ≃ 1/(F-1) ≃ 1/F .

Pointwise ρN=0.10 is μ²0=L/0.10=10, i.e. E[F]≃1+10=11, the
familiar F≈10 rule.

The operational 95 % statement used for the Nagar bias is the
weak instrument size calibration.  With k2=1

k2F →d χ²k2(μ²) ,

ρN is monotone decreasing in μ² and the 5 % size test of

H0 :  ρN≥0.10 ⇔ μ²≤μ²0=L/0.10=10

vs H1 : ρN<0.10

is

P{ F ≥ F* | μ²=μ²0 } =0.95 .

Hence F* is the 5 % left tail of the non central
χ²1(μ²0=10), i.e. the Stock–Yogo 10 % maximal relative bias 5 %
critical value,

F* = F0.95(1,∞;μ²=10) ≃ 16.38 ,

F-1 ≃ μ².  With Fobs ≳ F* we have
P{μ²≥10|Fobs}≈0.95 and hence P{ρN=1/μ²≤0.10|Fobs}≈0.95 in the
Nagar/Stock–Yogo maximal relative bias sense.  In practice this is
quoted as the F>10 rule made 95% confident, F*≈16–17, ≈16 to the
nearest whole number, with ρN≈1/(F-1)≈0.067 at F=16.

Remark.  The direct normal fiducial lower bound for the
concentration parameter obtained from the weak instrument
approximation

T=√F ≃ N(√μ²,1) ,

√μ²L ≃ √F - z1-α ,  μ²L ≃ (√F - z1-α)² ,
ρNU ≃ μL⁻² ≃ (√F - z1-α)⁻² ,

is √F1-α = z1-α+√10. With the one sided 95 % normal quantile
z0.95=1.645,

√F0.95 ≃ √10+1.645 ≃4.81 ,   F0.95 ≃(√10+1.645)²≃23.1,

F-1≳(√10+1.645)² i.e. F≳24–25 on the usual μ²≃F-1 scale, and
F0.95²ˢᵈ≃(√10+1.96)²≃26.2≈26 with the conventional two-sided
z0.975.  This is the √F≈N(√μ²,1) 95 % lower confidence bound for
μ²>10, the 20–30 safety factor that sits on top of the
Stock–Yogo size-controlled critical value F*SY≈16.4 quoted above.

6.text:
With $L=1$ the homoskedastic first order Nagar bias on the OLS scale is

${\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]\simeq \sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}L\mu^{-2}$,
${\rm plim}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]=\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}$,

so that on the Nagar scale

$\rho_{N}(\mu^{2})\simeq L\mu^{-2}\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq (F-1)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1}$,
$F\simeq1+\mu^{2}/L$,

and the point Nagar $10\%$ rule is $\rho_{N}=0.10\iff\mu^{2}=L/0.10=10$,
i.e. $F_{med}\simeq1+10\simeq11$, the familiar $F\approx10$ rule.

In the weak instrument limit with normal errors

$T:=\sqrt F\;\stackrel{a}{\sim}\;N\!\big(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\big),\qquad 
F\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ ,

so that up to the $+1$ in $F\simeq1+\mu^{2}$ a $1-\alpha$ fiducial lower
bound for the concentration parameter can be written as

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\simeq \sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha},\qquad 
\mu^{2}_{L}\simeq\big(\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}\big)^{2},$

and

$\rho_{N}^{U,1-\alpha}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}\simeq\big(\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}\big)^{-2}$

is a $1-\alpha$ upper bound for the Nagar relative bias.  Putting
$\rho_{N}^{U}=0.10$, i.e. $\mu_{L}^{2}=10$,

$\sqrt{F_{1-\alpha}}=z_{1-\alpha}+\sqrt{10}$ .

With the one sided $95\%$ normal quantile $z_{0.95}=1.645$

$\sqrt{F_{0.95}}\simeq3.162+1.645=4.81$,
$F_{0.95}\simeq\big(\sqrt{10}+1.645\big)^{2}\simeq23.1$,

i.e. an observed first stage $F\approx22\!-\!24$ puts the $95\%$ one
sided lower fiducial limit $\mu^{2}_{L}\ge10$ and hence a $95\%$ upper
limit $\rho_{N}\lesssim0.10$.  On the usual small sample
$\mu^{2}\simeq F-1$ scale this is $F-1\gtrsim(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}$,
$F\gtrsim24\!-\!25$, and with the conventional two sided
$z_{0.975}=1.96$ normalisation

$F_{0.95}^{2sd}\simeq(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\simeq26.2\approx26$,

the $F\approx10$ point Nagar rule inflated by the $\sim1.6\!-\!2.0$
s.e. safety factor for $t=\sqrt F$.  That is the direct $95\%$ lower
confidence bound for $\mu^{2}>10$.

Remark.  The operational weak-instrument size calibration that is
normally quoted in the Nagar/Stock-Yogo literature is the inversion

${\rm P}\!\left[F\ge F^{*}\mid\mu^{2}_{0}=L/0.10\right]=0.95$,

i.e. the $5\%$ size test of $H_{0}:\rho_{N}\ge0.10$.  With $k_{2}=L=1$,
$\mu^{2}_{0}=10$,

$F^{*}_{SY}=F_{0.95}\!\left(1,\infty;\mu^{2}=10\right)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17,$

so that $F\approx16$ is the conventional $10\%$ maximal relative bias
$5\%$ size / $95\%$ confidence threshold, the $F>10$ rule made
$95\%$ confident in the Stock-Yogo maximal-relative-bias sense.  On the
$F-1$ scale this is $\rho_{N}\approx1/(F-1)\approx0.067$ at $F\approx16$.
∎

10.text:
In the homoskedastic just identified case with $L=1$

$${\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]\simeq 
\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}\frac{L}{\mu^{2}},\qquad 
{\rm plim}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]=\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}$$

so on the Nagar scale

$$\rho_{N}(\mu^{2})\equiv
\frac{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]}
     {{\rm plim}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]}
\simeq\frac{L}{\mu^{2}}\simeq\frac1{\mu^{2}}\simeq
\frac1{F-1}\simeq\frac1F ,
\qquad F\simeq 1+\mu^{2}$$

pointwise $\rho_{N}=0.10\iff \mu^{2}=L/0.10=10\iff
F_{med}\simeq 1+10\simeq 11$, the familiar $F\approx10$ rule.

In weak instrument asymptotics with normal errors

$$T:=\sqrt F\;\stackrel{a}{\sim}\;N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right),
\qquad F\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2}) , $$

so that up to first order a $1-\alpha$ lower fiducial bound for the
concentration parameter is

$$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\simeq T-z_{1-\alpha},\qquad
\mu^{2}_{L}\simeq\bigl(\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr)^{2}, $$

and

$$\rho_{N}^{U,1-\alpha}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}
    \simeq\bigl[\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr]^{-2} $$

is a $1-\alpha$ upper bound for the Nagar relative bias.  Putting
$\rho_{N}^{U}=0.10$, i.e. $\mu_{L}^{2}=10$,

$$\sqrt{F_{1-\alpha}}=z_{1-\alpha}+\sqrt{10}. $$

On the usual one sided 95$\%$ normal normalisation $z_{0.95}=1.645$

$$\sqrt{F_{0.95}}\simeq\sqrt{10}+1.645\simeq3.162+1.645=4.81,$$
$$F_{0.95}\simeq\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\simeq23.1, $$

i.e. an observed $F\approx 22\!-\!24$ puts the 95$\%$ one sided lower
fiducial limit $\mu_{L}^{2}\ge 10$ and hence a 95$\%$ upper limit
$\rho_{N}\lesssim0.10$ on the Nagar relative bias.  On the conventional
small sample $\mu^{2}\simeq F-1$ scale this is

$$F-1\gtrsim\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2},\qquad 
F\gtrsim 24\!-\!25, $$

and with the textbook two sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ normalisation

$$F_{0.95}^{2sd}\simeq\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.96\bigr)^{2}\simeq26.2\approx26,$$

the $F\approx10$ point Nagar rule inflated by the $\approx1.6\!-\!2.0$
s.e. safety factor for the sampling variation of $T=\sqrt F$.

Remark.  The size controlled Stock–Yogo inversion

$${\rm P}\!\left\{F\ge F^{*}\mid\mu^{2}_{0}=L/0.10=10\right\}=0.95, $$

$F\,|\,\mu^{2}\sim\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$, is the conventional operational
weak-instrument calibration.  For $k_{2}=L=1$,

$$F^{*}_{SY}=F_{0.95}\!\left(1,\infty;\mu^{2}=10\right)\simeq16.38\approx16\!-\!17, $$

i.e. $F\approx16$ on the $F-1\simeq\mu^{2}$ scale, the $F>10$ point Nagar
rule made $5\%$ size/$95\%$ confident in the Stock–Yogo maximal-relative-
bias sense, $\rho_{N}\simeq1/(F-1)\simeq0.067$ at $F=16$.  This is the
$F\approx16$ value usually quoted in the literature; the $F\approx23\!-\!26$
numbers above are the direct $95\%$ lower confidence bound for
$\mu^{2}>10$ under the $\sqrt F\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ fiducial
approximation. ∎

11.text:
With one endogenous regressor and one instrument the homoskedastic
Nagar first order bias on the OLS scale is

${\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]\simeq 
\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}\,L\mu^{-2}$ ,   $L=1$,

${\rm plim}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]=\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}$,

so that on the Nagar scale

$\rho_{N}(\mu^{2})\equiv 
\frac{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]}
     {{\rm plim}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]}\simeq\frac{L}{\mu^{2}}
     \simeq\frac1{\mu^{2}}\simeq\frac1{F-1}\simeq\frac1F$ ,
$F\simeq1+\mu^{2}/L$ ,

$T:=\sqrt F\stackrel{a}{\sim}N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right)$,

Hence up to the $+1$ in $F\simeq1+\mu^{2}$ a $1-\alpha$ fiducial
lower bound for the concentration parameter is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\simeq\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}$,
$\mu^{2}_{L}\simeq\bigl(\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr)^{2}$,

and

$\rho_{N}^{U,1-\alpha}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}\simeq
\bigl[\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr]^{-2}$

is a $1-\alpha$ upper bound for the Nagar relative bias.  Putting
$\rho_{N}^{U}=0.10$, i.e. $\mu_{L}^{2}=1/0.10=10$,

$\sqrt{F_{1-\alpha}}=z_{1-\alpha}+\sqrt{10}$ .

On the $F\simeq\mu^{2}$ normalisation the one-sided $95\%$ normal
bound is therefore

$\sqrt{F_{0.95}}=\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}\approx3.162+1.645=4.807$
$\;,$

$F_{0.95}\simeq(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx23.1$,

i.e. an observed $F\approx22\!-\!24$ puts the $95\%$ one-sided lower
fiducial limit $\mu^{2}_{L}\ge10$ and hence a $95\%$ upper limit

$\mu^{2}\simeq F-1$ scale this is $F-1\gtrsim(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}$,
$F\gtrsim24\!-\!25$, and with the conventional two-sided $95\%$
normal quantile $z_{0.975}=1.96$

$F_{0.95}^{2sd}\simeq(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26.2\approx26$,

the familiar $F\approx10$ point Nagar rule inflated by the
$\approx1.6\!-\!2.0$ s.e. safety factor for the first-stage $t=\sqrt F$.
The median point Nagar rule is $\rho_{N}\simeq1/F=0.10\iff
F\approx10$, $F-1\approx10\iff F\approx11$.

Remark.  The size-controlled operationalisation used in the weak
instrument literature inverts the non-central law
$P\{F\ge F^{*}|\mu^{2}=L/0.10\}=0.95$, i.e.

${\rm P}\{F\ge F^{*}|\mu^{2}_{0}=10\}=0.95$,

$F^{*}=F_{0.95}\!\left(1,\infty;\mu^{2}=10\right)\approx16.38\approx
16\!-\!17$,

the Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal relative bias $5\%$ size critical value.
That is the $F>10$ point rule made $5\%$ size/$95\%$ confident in the
usual Stock–Yogo maximal-bias sense, $F^{*}\approx16.4$ $\approx16$
to the nearest whole number, $\rho_{N}\approx1/(F-1)\approx0.067$ at
$F=16$.  The $\approx23\!-\!26$ numbers above are the direct
$\sqrt F\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ fiducial $95\%$ lower confidence
bound for $\mu^{2}>10$ itself.

public_text.7:
The Nagar bias on the OLS scale is RelBias_N ≃ L/μ² with L=1, and in the weak-instrument normal limit

F ≃ 1+μ² ,   T := √F  ≃ N(√μ² ,1).

Hence up to the usual F-1 shift a 1-α upper bound for the Nagar relative bias is

ρ_N^{U} ≃ μ_L^{-2} ≃ [√F - z_{1-α}]^{-2},     √μ²_L ≃ √F - z_{1-α}.

The 10% bias level is μ²_L = L/0.10 =10. Putting ρ_N^{U}=0.10,

√F_{1-α}= z_{1-α}+ √10 .

That is the direct fiducial lower confidence bound for the concentration parameter, μ²_L >10 ⇔ ρ_N <0.10.

The question is a 95% confidence statement for μ². Confidence for a normal mean is conventionally two-sided. For T≈N(√μ²,1) the usual 95% two-sided interval is ±z_{0.975}=1.96, i.e. the one-sided lower 2.5% quantile. Using z_{0.95}=1.645 gives a 90% two-sided, 95% one-sided interval, which is the 1.645 bound that is often quoted as the “one-sided 95%” shortcut.

Sampling variation of the first stage is the point of contention. Under weak instrument asymptotics kF∼χ²_k(μ²). With k=1, √F≈N(√μ²,1) to first order, so a normal fiducial lower bound is √μ²_L≈√F−z1-α and μ²_L≈(√F−z1-α)². Requiring the 1-α upper bound for RelBias=1/μ²_L to be 0.10, i.e. μ²_L=10, gives √F1-α=√10+z1-α. With the one-sided 95% normal quantile z0.95=1.645 this is F≈(3.162+1.645)²≈23.1, ≈24–25 on the F-1≈μ² scale, and with the conventional two-sided z0.975=1.96, F≈(3.162+1.96)²≈26.2≈26. This is the direct √F≈N(√μ²,1) Taylor/delta-method 95% lower confidence bound for μ²>10, i.e. the ≈20–30 safety factor on top of the point F≈10 rule.

Distinct from that is the Stock-Yogo weak instrument size inversion. Under weak instrument asymptotics the 5% size test of H0: maximal Nagar relative bias ≥0.10 ⇔ μ²≤μ²0=L/0.10=10 vs H1: maximal relative bias<0.10 is P[F≥F*|μ²=10]=0.95. For k=L=1 this is the 95th percentile of χ²1(10), F* = F0.95(1,∞; μ²=10)≈16.38≈16–17, conventionally quoted as F≈16, with RelBias≈1/(F-1)≈0.067 at that point. This is the operational “95% confident / 5% size” maximal relative bias calibration used in the literature.

confident.

With one endogenous regressor and one instrument under homoskedasticity the first order Nagar relative bias on the OLS scale is

ρ_N ≃ L/μ² ,  L=1 ,   μ² = π′Z′Zπ/σ_v²

and in the weak instrument limit k₂F →ᵈ χ²_{k₂}(μ²) with k₂ =1, so that in large samples F ≃ 1+ μ² and ρ_N ≃ 1/(F-1) ≃ 1/F.

Pointwise ρ_N =0.10 is μ²₀ = L/0.10 =10, i.e. the familiar F≈10-11 mean Nagar rule. The frequentist statement “ρ_N <0.10 with 95% confidence’’ used in the weak instrument literature is the size calibration of Stock–Yogo. ρ_N is monotone decreasing in μ² so the 5% size test of

H₀ : maximal relative bias ≥0.10 ⇔ μ² ≤ μ²₀=10
vs H₁ : maximal relative bias <0.10

is the non-central inversion

P[ F ≥ F* | μ² = μ²₀ ] =0.95 .

That is P{ F ≥ F* | μ² =10}=0.95, i.e. the 5% left tail of the first stage under the null maximal relative bias. With k₂=L=1

F* = F_{0.95}(1,∞; μ²=10)

the 95th percentile of χ²₁(10). Inverting the non-central χ² gives

F* ≃ 16.38

commonly quoted as F≈16-17, ≈16 to the nearest whole number. With F_obs ≥ F* we have P{ μ² ≥10 | F_obs }≈0.95 and hence P{ ρ_N =1/μ² ≤0.10 | F_obs }≈0.95 in the Nagar/Stock–Yogo maximal relative bias sense. On the usual μ²≃F-1 scale ρ_N≃1/(F-1)≈0.067 at F≈16, i.e. the F>10 rule made 5% size /95% confident.

The √F≈N(√μ²,1) fiducial bound √μ²_L≈√F−z_{1-α}, μ²_L≈(√F−z_{1-α})² and the resulting √F_{1-α}=z_{1-α}+√10 → F≈(√10+1.645)²≈23.1, 24-26 with F-1 and z_{0.975}, is a normal delta-method lower confidence limit for the concentration parameter itself. It replaces the non-central χ²₁(μ²) law by a normal approximation to √F, squares the bound for √μ² and then plugs it into the non-linear map 1/μ². At μ²=10 the non-central χ²₁ is markedly skewed, the normal approximation to √F is only first order accurate for large μ², and the bound double counts sampling variation. It is a useful safety factor for μ²_L>10, not the size-controlled inversion P[F≥F*|μ²=10]=0.95 that defines 95% confidence for the Nagar relative bias.

That is why the textbook operationalisation of “95% confident that the asymptotic Nagar relative bias is <10% of the OLS bias’’ with one instrument is the Stock–Yogo 10% maximal relative bias 5% size critical value F*≈16.38, i.e. F≈16 on an integer scale, the conventional F>10 rule made 95% confident.

is

${\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]\simeq\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}L\mu^{-2}$,
${\rm plim}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]=\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}$, 

so that on the Nagar scale

$\rho_{N}(\mu^{2})\simeq L\mu^{-2}\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq\frac1{F-1}
\simeq\frac1F$,  $F\simeq1+\mu^{2}$,

and point wise $\rho_{N}=0.10\iff\mu^{2}_{0}=L/0.10=10\iff F_{med}

vs $H_{1}:\rho_{N}<0.10$

is

${\rm P}\{F\ge F^{*}\mid\mu^{2}=\mu^{2}_{0}\}=0.95$,

i.e. $F^{*}$ is the $5\%$ left tail of the first stage under the null

$F^{*}_{SY}\simeq16.38\approx16\!-\!17,$

scale $\rho_{N}\simeq1/(F-1)\simeq0.067$ at $F\simeq16$.

critical value, the $F>10$ rule made $95\%$ confident, $F^{*}\approx16$
to the nearest integer.  The $F\approx16\!-\!17$ value is the textbook
Stock–Yogo operational threshold.
